module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Dubner's conjecture

*Reference*: [Every even number greater than 4208 is the sum of two t-primes](https://scispace.com/pdf/twin-prime-conjectures-3icaxy6b0m.pdf)
by *Harvey Dubner*.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace DubnerConjecture

/--
A twin prime is a prime number that has a prime gap of 2, meaning either p - 2 or p + 2
is also prime.
-/
def IsTwinPrime (p : ℕ) : Prop :=
  p.Prime ∧ ((p - 2).Prime ∨ (p + 2).Prime)

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem t1 : ¬IsTwinPrime 2 := by
  norm_num [IsTwinPrime]

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem t2 : IsTwinPrime 3 := by
  norm_num [IsTwinPrime]

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem t3 : IsTwinPrime 5 := by
  norm_num [IsTwinPrime]

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem t4 : IsTwinPrime 101 := by
  norm_num [IsTwinPrime]

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem t5 : ¬IsTwinPrime 100 := by
  norm_num [IsTwinPrime]

/--
Every even number greater than 4208 is the sum of two twin primes.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem dubner_conjecture (n : ℕ) (hn : 4208 < n) (h : Even n) :
    ∃ p q : ℕ,
      IsTwinPrime p ∧
      IsTwinPrime q ∧
      p + q = n := by
  sorry

end DubnerConjecture

reformulations.difference: The source defines a t-prime as "a prime which has a twin" (another prime at distance 2). The Lean writes this as `p.Prime ∧ ((p - 2).Prime ∨ (p + 2).Prime)`, with truncated ℕ subtraction in `p - 2`. That is a known Lean pitfall a reader might worry about, e.g. at p = 2 or p = 3.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Truncation never changes the answer. Any prime p is at least 2. For p = 2, p - 2 = 0 exactly (not prime) and p + 2 = 4 (not prime), so 2 is correctly excluded. For p ≥ 2, p - 2 is the exact difference. I proved in Lean `IsTwinPrime p ↔ p.Prime ∧ ∃ q, q.Prime ∧ ((q:ℤ) - p = 2 ∨ (p:ℤ) - q = 2)`. From it I derived the equivalence of `dubner_conjecture` with the source's Conjecture 4a stated over positive integers with the ℤ-difference twin notion. Computationally, the file's definition lists the t-primes 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 29, 31, 41, … (OEIS A001097). For even n ≤ 30000 it reproduces exactly the OEIS A007534 exception list 2, 4, 94, 96, 98, …, 4204, 4206, 4208 (plus 0).

sources_consulted: https://scispace.com/pdf/twin-prime-conjectures-3icaxy6b0m.pdf (the cited link; blocked by an AWS WAF JavaScript challenge, with no Wayback snapshot, so I could not read it there)
https://oeis.org/A007534/a007534.pdf (Harvey Dubner, 'Twin Prime Conjectures', J. Recreational Math. 30(3), 1999-2000; scan hosted by OEIS; I extracted and read all 6 pages)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02381 and its e-print TeX source (T. Pandey, 'An intermediate conjecture between Goldbach and Dubner', 2026)
review.notes:
No misformalization found. The file states Dubner's Conjecture 4a faithfully.

**Source check.** The cited scispace PDF is behind a bot challenge. I read the same paper through the OEIS-hosted scan (https://oeis.org/A007534/a007534.pdf), which Wikipedia and Pandey 2026 also cite.
- p. 1: "A t-prime is defined as a prime which has a twin."
- p. 2: "Conjecture 4a: Every even number greater than 4208 is the sum of two t-primes."
- `dubner_conjecture` (∀ n, 4208 < n → Even n → ∃ p q, IsTwinPrime p ∧ IsTwinPrime q ∧ p + q = n) is exactly this. The strict bound matches "greater than".
- Equal summands are allowed in the source, and the Lean allows p = q too:
  - page 2 writes the analogous equation as N = m1 + m2 with m1 ≤ m2 (the ≤ glyph is CMSY10 character 20);
  - Table 1 counts 12 = 6 + 6 as a hit;
  - the Mathematica code in OEIS A007534 sums over all index pairs, including i = j.
- Pandey 2026 restates the definition the same way: "Call a prime t a twin member if t − 2 or t + 2 is prime… every even n > 4208 is a sum of two twin members".

**Lean experiments (scratch files only; the checkout was not modified).**
- `#eval` with the file's `IsTwinPrime`: the even n ≤ 30000 with no representation are exactly {0, 2, 4, 94, …, 4204, 4206, 4208}. This matches A007534, plus 0.
- I proved that 4208 has no representation (using `native_decide`, scratch only). So the bound is tight, and `4207 < n` would be false.
- I proved that 4210 = 191 + 4019 is representable. The hypotheses can be satisfied, so the statement is not vacuous.
- I proved that the statement implies there are infinitely many twin primes. So it cannot be settled easily, and `research open` is appropriate.
- The tests t1–t5 are correct: 2 is not a t-prime; 3, 5 and 101 are; 100 is not.

**Status.** Still open.
- Dubner (2000): "It is not reasonable to expect these conjectures to be proved true in the near future. Their truth would imply an infinite number of twin primes as well as the truth of the Goldbach conjecture."
- OEIS (September 2026): "Conjectured to be complete… No other k < 10^11."
- Pandey (arXiv:2608.02381, August 2026) verifies it up to 10^11 and treats it as open.

**Cosmetic points, not reported as findings.**
- The module docstring's link text is the conjecture statement, not the paper's title ('Twin Prime Conjectures', J. Recreational Math. 30(3), 1999–2000).
- The scispace link is not reachable without JavaScript. The OEIS-hosted scan would be a more stable reference.
- Only Conjecture 4a is formalized. The paper's other conjectures (1, 2, 3, 3a, 4) are not; that is not a defect.
